A normative calculator for MoCA domain 
scores: proxy for Z‑scores of conventional 
neuropsychological tests
Tau Ming Liew1,2,3,4* 
Abstract 
Background  Test items in MoCA (Montreal Cognitive Assessment) can be used to generate 5 domain scores (i.e. 
Memory, Language, Attention, Executive and Visuospatial) which have been shown to approximate well-established 
neuropsychological tests. As neuropsychological tests are known to be affected by age, sex, education, and language 
of administration, this study derived a regression-based Z-score calculator for MoCA Domain Scores (MDS) that adjusts 
individual performance for these key confounders; with the intention of improving the clinical utility of MDS 
as a proxy for conventional neuropsychological tests.
Methods  Participants ≥ 50 years were recruited from Alzheimer’s Disease Centers across USA (n = 25,330), and com-
pleted MoCA and conventional neuropsychological tests. A subset with normal cognition and global Clinical Demen-
tia Rating of 0 (n = 11,371) was used to derive the Z-score calculator for MDS; while the full sample (n = 25,330) verified 
the performance of MDS Z-scores in detecting domain-specific impairments (as defined by conventional neuropsy-
chological tests), using areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC).
Results  MDS varied significantly by age, sex, education, and language of administration even among participants 
with normal cognition. Based on age-, sex-, education-, and language-adjusted Z-scores, the respective AUCs were 
91.2% for MoCA–Memory (95%CI 90.7–91.6), 83.6% for MoCA–Language (95%CI 83.0–84.3), 88.7% for MoCA–Atten-
tion (95%CI 88.0–89.4), 85.5% for MoCA–Executive (95%CI 84.8–86.1), and 81.0% for MoCA–Visuospatial (95%CI 
80.2–81.8). At the commonly-used cut-off of Z-scores ≤ -1.50, all the MDS had specificities of ≥ 80%.
Conclusions  MDS Z-scores can be easily computed using the newly-developed Excel-based calculator, and provide 
a viable alternative when conventional neuropsychological tests are needed but cannot be feasibly administered, 
such as in non-specialty clinics with large volume of patients at high-risk of cognitive impairment (e.g. primary-care, 
geriatric, and stroke-prevention clinics), and, with further validation and calibration, plausibly also in other resource-
limited healthcare settings (e.g. in lower- and middle-income countries). They can complement neuropsychologi-
cal tests as part of the systematic evaluation of cognitive impairment, and help reserve neuropsychological tests 
for patients most likely to benefit from further evaluation.

Introduction
Conventional neuropsychological testing plays an essen-
tial role in the clinical assessment of cognitive impair-
ment [1, 2]. It is a key component in the diagnosis of 
cognitive impairment, given that most of the diagnos-
tic criteria for mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and 
dementia require demonstrable impairment in at least 
one or more cognitive domains [3]. Neuropsychological 
testing also helps identify subtypes of cognitive impair-
ment – by distinguishing neuropsychological profiles 
associated with various subtypes, as well as demonstrat-
ing consistency of these profiles with neuroimaging find-
ings [1]. However, neuropsychological testing is often 
time-consuming to administer and may not be suited 
for routine use in clinical practices with high volume of 
patients. Moreover, neuropsychological testing can only 
be conducted by specialized, trained personnel, making it 
less accessible to general clinicians outside of specialized 
memory clinics or in resource-limited healthcare settings 
(e.g. those in lower- and middle-income countries). Con-
sequently, much of the diagnostic process for cognitive 
impairment to date still relies on bedside cognitive tests 
[3], among which the Montreal Cognitive Assessment 
(MoCA) [4] is one of the most widely-used [5].
The widespread adoption of MoCA is understand-
able, given its many desirable features [6–8] –MoCA 
can be completed in 10–15 min, is available for clinical 
use  without licensing fee, has been translated into > 50 
languages [9], covers the key cognitive domains relevant 
to cognitive impairment (including robust measures of 
visuospatial and executive function), and demonstrates 
acceptable performance in detecting early cognitive 
impairment [4, 5]. Given MoCA’s widespread use and 
meaningful coverage of key cognitive domains, there has 
been growing to examine whether MoCA’s test items can 
be used to derive domain scores that measure individu-
als’ abilities across different cognitive domains. In recent 
literature, Julayanont et  al. took reference from pub-
lished neuropsychological and neuroimaging evidence 
[10], and proposed a set of MoCA domain scores (MDS) 
that utilizes individual items in MoCA to determine the 
cognitive performance in 5 key domains: Memory, Lan-
guage, Attention, Executive, and Visuospatial abilities. 
The detailed calculations for these 5 domains of MDS 
are presented in Table 1. Most recently, a study by Ang 
et al. [11] demonstrated the validity of these 5 domains 
of MDS in a large US sample (n = 14,571), showing that 
MDS approximate well-established neuropsychological 
tests and discriminate among various subtypes of early 
cognitive impairment.
Notwithstanding the promise, MDS are currently only 
available as raw scores, which can pose challenges for 
clinical interpretation. Given that neuropsychological 
test performance is well-known to be affected by age, 
sex, educational attainment, and language of admin-
istration [2, 12–14], the raw scores do not account for 
normal variations related to these factors. As a result, 
clinicians interpreting MDS raw scores must arbitrarily 
decide whether a particular set of scores falls within the 
normal range for someone of a given age, sex, educa-
tional attainment, and language of administration. This 
approach increases subjectivity in interpretation and 
may inadvertently create false positive or false nega-
tive results when clinicians over- or under-interpret the 
raw scores. To minimize such challenge and potentially 
improve the clinical utility of MDS, this study sought 
to:
1)	 Derive a regression-based normative calculator that 
could yield estimates of age-, sex-, education, and 
language-adjusted Z-scores and percentile ranges; 
and
2)	 Demonstrate the performance of MDS Z-scores in 
detecting impairment in the respective cognitive 
domains of memory, language, attention, executive 
function, and visuospatial abilities.
Methods
Study population
The study involved participants recruited from 39 Alz-
heimer’s Disease Centers (ADCs) across USA, as avail-
able in the National Alzheimer’s Coordinating Center 
(NACC) database [15]. It included participants who ful-
filled the following criteria: (1) available in the NACC 
database from March 2015 (the date when MoCA was 
first introduced in NACC database) to November 2023; 
and (2) aged ≥ 50 years. For participants who contrib-
uted more than 1 set of data (due to multiple follow-
up visits), only the first set of data was included in the 
study. Of note, the study did not exclude participants 
with missing or incomplete data on MDS; this approach 
was intentional to minimize the issue of selection bias, 
given that those who could not complete the cognitive 
tests usually represent a distinctive subgroup of individ-
uals, and the exclusion of this subgroup of participants 
may potentially bias the findings on MDS’s perfor-
mance. Instead, the study adopted robust methods to 
address missing or incomplete data on MDS, through 
the conduct of multiple imputation and sensitivity 
analyses which are further described in the Statistical 
Analyses section below. The ADCs obtained informed 
consent from participants, and received approval by 
their local institutional review boards. Research using

Measures
The MoCA used in this study was based on version 
7.1 [4]. Only three language options were available for 
MoCA administration in NACC, namely English, Span-
ish and Chinese, as these were the only languages avail-
able in NACC’s data collection forms. Notwithstanding 
this, each participant’s native language was also recorded, 
and used to determine whether MoCA was administered 
in participant’s native language.
The MoCA domain scores (MDS) were previously pro-
posed by Julayanont et  al. [10], using individual items 
in MoCA to derive scores for 5 cognitive domains. The 
detailed calculations of MDS are shown in Table  1. 
Briefly, the 5 domains of MDS (and in parentheses, their 
corresponding MoCA items) are: (1) MoCA–Memory 
(Delayed Recall–No Cue, Delayed Recall–Category Cue, 
and Delayed Recall–Recognition); (2) MoCA–Language 
(Picture Naming, Sentence Repetition, and Letter Flu-
ency); (3) MoCA–Attention (Five-Word Registration, 
Digit Span, Letter Tapping, Serial-7 Subtraction, and 
Sentence Repetition); (4) MoCA–Executive (Trail Mak-
ing, Clock Drawing, Digit Span, Letter Tapping, Serial-7 
Subtraction, Letter Fluency, and Abstraction); and (5) 
MoCA–Visuospatial (Cube Copy, Clock Drawing, and 
Picture Naming). Of note, the original MoCA–Memory 
and MoCA–Attention by Julayanont et al. [10] included 
auxiliary items that are not part of MoCA total score (i.e. 
Five-Word Registration, Delayed Recall–Category Cue, 
and Delayed Recall–Recognition). As these auxiliary

this study also explored the omission of the auxiliary 
items from MoCA–Memory and MoCA–Attention to 
constitute shorter versions of MoCA–Memory (short) 
and MoCA–Attention (short). The calculations of these 
shorter versions are also shown in Table 1.
Conventional neuropsychological testing in this study 
included eight tests measuring the 5 key cognitive 
domains: (1) delayed memory (Craft Story 21 Delayed 
Recall and Benson Complex Figure Recall) [16, 17]; (2) 
language (Multilingual Naming Test and Verbal Fluency–
Animal) [18, 19]; (3) attention (Number Span Test For-
ward and Backward) [20]; (4) executive function (Trail 
Making Test Part B) [21]; and (5) visuospatial abilities 
(Benson Complex Figure Copy) [17]. Further descrip-
tions of the neuropsychological tests are also available 
in Supplementary Material 1. Score for each neuropsy-
chological test was converted to age-, sex- and educa-
tion-adjusted Z-score based on published calculator for 
NACC cohort [12]. In domains that were measured by > 1 
neuropsychological tests, the Z-scores for the neuropsy-
chological tests were averaged to produce the domain 
Z-scores [22–25]. Consistent with recent practices in the 
literature, domain Z-scores of ≤ -1.50 were used to define 
the presence of impairment in the respective domains 
[22–25].
The clinical diagnoses were made based on all available 
information from standardized assessments, with 81.8% 
made via consensus conference and the remainder made 
by single clinicians. Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) 
was diagnosed using modified Petersen criteria [26], and 
dementia was diagnosed with McKhann (2011) criteria 
[27]. Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR® Dementia Staging 
Instrument) [28] is used to determine the staging of cog-
nitive impairment. It is based on rating from 6 domains 
(memory, orientation, judgment and problem solving, 
community affairs, home and hobbies, and personal 
care), which can be totalled to yield a CDR sum of boxes 
score (ranging from 0 to 18), or converted to a global 
CDR score based on published rules [28] to indicate the 
severity of cognitive impairment (0 = normal cognition, 
0.5 = questionable cognitive impairment, 1 = mild demen-
tia, 2 = moderate dementia, and 3 = severe dementia).
Statistical analyses
Aim (1) sought to derive a normative Z-score calcula-
tor for MDS using a well-established regression-based 
approach [12, 29]. Taking reference from previously pub-
lished methods [12, 29], this analysis was conducted in 
the subset of sample with normal cognition and global 
CDR of 0 (denoted as normative dataset), using the fol-
lowing equation:

tions and k as the number of predictors (including

standard deviation of the residuals, and is often 
included as a standard output of linear regression 
models in most statistical softwares.
Aim (2) sought to verify the performance of MDS 
Z-scores in detecting the respective domain-specific 
impairments (defined by domain Z-scores of ≤ -1.50 on 
conventional neuropsychological tests; consistent with 
recent practices in the literature) [22–25]. This analy-
sis was conducted in the full sample, by computing area 
under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). 
In general, an AUC of 0.7–0.8 is considered acceptable 
discrimination, 0.8–0.9 is considered excellent, and more 
than 0.9 is considered outstanding [30].
Multiple imputation was used during the analyses 
for Aim 1 and 2, to account for missing or incomplete 
data on MDS [31]. This is a robust and well-established 
approach to minimize biased results related to missing 
data. Unlike the traditional approach of complete records 
analyses (which exclude participants with missing 
data from the statistical analyses), multiple imputation 
acknowledges the presence of missing data and replaces 
them with plausible estimates (while accounting for the 
uncertainty introduced by missing data); thus ensuring 
that the statistical inferences are still representative of 
the whole study population and not unduly influenced by 
individuals with missing data. This approach is especially 
relevant when those with missing data represent a dis-
tinctive subgroup of individuals, whereby the exclusion 
of this subgroup of participants can reduce the repre-
sentativeness of the statistical inferences, and potentially 
distort or inflate the findings.

A comparison of demographics between participants 
with and without missing data is shown in Supplemen-
tary Material 2, of which those with missing data were 
older, had less education, more likely to be of other eth-
nicities (i.e. not White or African American), more likely 
to have the diagnosis of dementia, and had higher scores 
on CDR sum of boxes. The conduct of the multiple impu-
tation is further described in Supplementary Material 
3. Briefly, the multiple imputation utilizes Multivariate 
Imputation by Chained Equation (MICE) to ‘predict’ 
the values of missing data on MDS based on the other 
available variables in the study. One hundred imputa-
tion datasets were created to simulate the uncertainty 
in the imputed values. The statistical analyses were then 
conducted in each of the 100 imputed datasets, with the 
100 sets of corresponding results combined using Rubin’s 
rules [32].
Although multiple imputation was used in the main 
analyses, a sensitivity analysis was also conducted to 
assess robustness of the results when Aim 2 (examine 
the performance of MDS Z-scores) was repeated using 
the complete data (i.e. only focusing on participants with 
complete data on MDS and excluding those with missing 
data on MDS). All analyses were conducted in Stata (ver-
sion 16).
Results
A total of 25,330 participants were included in the study, 
with a mean age of 72.4 years and a mean education of 
15.8 years. Among the included participants, 12,539 
(49.5%) had normal cognition, 5,717 (22.6%) had MCI 
and 7,074 (27.9%) had dementia. The flow diagram on 
participant selection is presented in Fig. 1, while the par-
ticipant characteristics are shown in Table 2.
The normative dataset (i.e. the subset with normal cog-
nition and global CDR of 0) (n = 11,371) was used initially 
to derive a normative Z-score calculator for MDS. Sup-
plementary Material 4 shows the mean scores of MDS 
in the normative dataset, stratified by the subgroups 
of age, sex, education, language of MoCA administra-
tion, whether MoCA was administered in participant’s 
native language. In multivariable regression analyses 
(Table 3), MDS largely varied by age, sex education, lan-
guage of administration, and administration in native 
language (p < 0.05 for most of the MDS). Women per-
formed significantly better than men on MoCA–Mem-
ory, MoCA–Language, MoCA–Attention; but worse on

To facilitate the use of MDS Z-scores in routine 
clinical practice, an Excel-based calculator was cre-
ated along with this study as a simple way to convert 
the MDS raw scores to the corresponding age-, sex-, 
education, and language-adjusted Z-scores. Using the 
normative calculator, the MDS Z-scores were then gen-
erated for the full sample (n = 25,330) to examine their 
performance in detecting impairment in the respec-
tive cognitive domains. As seen in Table 4, the respec-
tive AUCs were 91.2% for MoCA–Memory, 83.6% for 
MoCA–Language, 88.7% for MoCA–Attention, 85.5% 
for MoCA–Executive, and 81.0% for MoCA–Visuospa-
tial. At the commonly-used cut-off of Z-scores ≤ -1.50, 
all the MDS had specificity statistics of ≥ 80%. At a 
more lenient cut-off of Z-scores ≤ -0.50, the sensitiv-
ity statistics rose above 80% for all the MDS, but with 
some trade-off to the specificity statistics.
As the original MoCA–Memory and MoCA–Attention 
included auxiliary items that are not part of MoCA total 
score (i.e. Five-Word Registration, Delayed Recall–Cat-
egory Cue, and Delayed Recall–Recognition), this study 
also explored the omission of the auxiliary items from 
MoCA–Memory and MoCA–Attention to constitute 
shorter versions of MoCA–Memory (short) and MoCA–
Attention (short). As seen in Table 4, the AUCs for these 
shorter versions of MoCA–Memory and MoCA–Atten-
tion still maintained excellent AUCs (88.7–89.2%). For 
comparison purposes, an updated Z-score calcula-
tor for MoCA total score was also generated using the 
normative dataset in this study (n = 11,371), of which 
the updated MoCA Z-scores showed a similar AUC of 
89.8% in detecting MCI and dementia in the full dataset 
(n = 25,330) (Table 4). The updated Z-score calculator for 
MoCA total score was also made available in the Excel-
based calculator as part of this study.
The results remained largely similar in the sensitivity 
analysis when the performance of MDS Z-scores were re-
examined in the 20,031 participants with complete data 
on MDS (i.e. excluding 5,229 participants with missing 
or incomplete data on MDS). The results of the sensi-
tivity analysis are presented in Supplementary Material 
5. Almost all the MDS still maintained excellent AUC 
of ≥ 80%, with the exception of MoCA–Visuospatial’s 
and MoCA–Executive’s AUC which dropped marginally 
below the 80% mark. Similar to the main results, all the 
MDS had specificity statistics of ≥ 80% at the commonly-
used cut-off of Z-scores ≤ -1.50; while the sensitivity sta-
tistics rose above 80% for all MDS at the more lenient 
cut-off of Z-scores ≤ -0.50.
Discussion
To improve the clinical utility of MDS, this study devel-
oped an Excel-based calculator that converts raw scores 
of MDS to age-, sex-, education-, and language-adjusted 
Z-scores, approximating those of conventional neu-
ropsychological tests. Of the five MDS, MoCA–Memory 
showed outstanding performance in detecting domain-
specific impairment (AUC 91.2%), while the remaining 
MDS (i.e. MoCA–Language, MoCA–Attention, MoCA–
Executive, and MoCA–Visuospatial) demonstrated excel-
lent performance, with AUCs ranging from 81.0% to 
88.7%. By comparison, the performance of these MDS 
was largely similar to that of MoCA total score in detect-
ing MCI and dementia (AUC 89.8% based on updated 
Z-scores for MoCA total score). Shorter versions of 
MoCA–Memory and MoCA–Attention (omitting auxil-
iary MoCA items) also showed excellent AUCs (88.5%), 
albeit with marginal drop compared to the longer ver-
sions of MoCA–Memory and MoCA–Attention (which 
incorporated auxiliary items such as Five-Word Reg-
istration, Delayed Recall–Category Cue, and Delayed 
Recall–Recognition).
The findings are consistent with, and add on to, recent 
literature on the utility of MDS in approximating con-
ventional neuropsychological tests and in discriminating 
among the various subtypes of cognitive impairment [11, 
33–35]. Among the 5 domains of MDS, MoCA–Visuos-
patial showed more modest – albeit still excellent – per-
formance, possibly reflecting the inherent limitations 
of MoCA items in measuring the visuospatial domain. 
MoCA items contributing to the MoCA–Visuospatial 
score tend to assess more than one cognitive domain and 
may lack specificity for visuospatial abilities. For example, 
Clock Drawing, a key component in MoCA–Visuospa-
tial, measures both executive and visuospatial domains 
[11, 36]; so individuals with executive dysfunction but 
preserved visuospatial skills may score poorly on MoCA–
Visuospatial, leading to false positives. Similarly, Picture 
Naming, another key component of MoCA–Visuospa-
tial, measures both language and visuospatial domains; 
hence, low scores in Picture Naming may not necessarily 
indicate visuospatial impairment.
MDS offer several advantages over conventional neu-
ropsychological tests. MoCA requires only 10–15 min 
to administer (compared to 2–4 h for conventional neu-
ropsychological tests), and is available in multiple lan-
guages without a licensing fee [6–8]. It also provides 
clearly-prescribed and standardized instructions (avail-
able at www.​mocat​est.​org), and hence can be adminis-
tered even by non-clinicians as long as they have received 
sufficient training through the MoCA certification course 
[7]. Using the normative calculator from this study, the 
raw scores of MDS can be easily converted to age-, sex-,

This approach offers a viable alternative when conven-
tional neuropsychological testing is needed but cannot 
be feasibly administered in clinical practice, due to prac-
tical reasons such as limited availability of neuropsy-
chologists, high costs of neuropsychological testing, or 
patients’ difficulties to complete lengthy assessments. 
It may be especially useful in non-specialty clinics (e.g. 
primary-care, geriatric and stroke-prevention clinics), 
where there is pressing need to detect early cognitive 
impairment among large numbers of high-risk patients 
with multimorbidity [8]. Subject to further validation and 
calibration, MDS may also have potential utility in other 
resource-limited healthcare settings, such as those in 
lower- and middle-income countries.
While MDS may not fully substitute for conventional 
neuropsychological tests, they can complement neu-
ropsychological testing in routine clinical practice, and 
potentially help to reserve neuropsychological testing 
for patients who are most likely to benefit from further 
evaluation. As shown in Table 4, MDS Z-scores of ≤ -1.50 
demonstrate good specificity (> 80%); hence, individuals 
scoring below this cut-off exhibit sufficient evidence of 
domain-specific impairments and may not require addi-
tional neuropsychological testing. However, this thresh-
old has poorer sensitivity compared to the alternate 
cut-off of Z-scores ≤ -0.50, which achieves better sensi-
tivity (> 80%). This suggests that patients with Z-scores 
between -0.50 and -1.50 could still have domain-spe-
cific impairments and may require neuropsychological 
assessment, especially in the context of strong clinical 
suspicion. A proposed approach – incorporating MDS 
as part of the systematic evaluation of cognitive impair-
ment – is illustrated in the workflow in Fig. 2. Essentially, 
this approach “repurposes” a widely used cognitive test 
(i.e. MoCA), shifting its original intent as a screening 
tool for detecting cognitive impairment [4] to a prelimi-
nary tool that may also help differentiate among various 
subtypes of cognitive impairment. Given that MoCA is 
already extensively used in most clinical settings [5], this 
approach could conserve limited healthcare resources 
related to neuropsychological assessments and facilitate 
the appropriate referral of patients who are more likely to 
benefit from comprehensive neuropsychological evalua-
tion, e.g. ambiguous cases, those with very mild deficits, 
or situations where MDS could not provide conclusive 
profiling of the cognitive domains [11].
The findings should be considered in light of the 
strengths and limitations of this study. The study’s 
strengths include well-characterized samples (with 
standardized assessments and rigorous diagnostic evalu-
ations of cognitive impairment) and a large number of 
participants recruited from across USA [31]. However, 
several limitations should also be noted. First, partici-
pants in the study involved those who volunteered at 
the ADCs, which may explain the higher prevalence of 
dementia (27.9%) compared to rates commonly reported 
in community-settings. Given this limitation, the findings 
are probably less generalizable to patients in community 
settings, and more applicable to patients in ambulatory 
care settings where individuals often present voluntarily 
(i.e. similar to the study participants) [37–39]. Second,

the normative dataset included a higher proportion of 
individuals who were white and highly educated [40]; 
hence, the normative calculator may be more useful in 
settings with similar demographics. While efforts have 
been made to minimize this limitation (through multi-
ple imputation to ensure inclusion of underrepresented 
groups, e.g. individuals who were older, had lower educa-
tion, and were from other ethnicities), future studies are 
needed to further expand the normative data to include 
a broader representation of demographic groups. Third, 
caution should be exercised when using the normative 
calculator outside the USA, especially in populations 
that differ substantially in terms of ethnicity, language, 
and cultural background. Ideally, separate calculators 
should be developed using normative data representa-
tive of these distinct populations. Fourth, despite the 
rigor of this study, the findings would still benefit from 
further validations in future research, including explo-
ration of the relationship between domain Z-scores and 
various dementia biomarkers. Fifth, while MDS expand 
clinicians’ armamentarium in the assessment of cogni-
tive impairment, they are not intended to replace other 
relevant investigations, such as conventional neuropsy-
chological tests (when a more detailed profile of cogni-
tive deficits is needed), neuroimaging, or cerebrospinal 
fluid analysis [1, 2, 41]. Sixth, although MDS has dem-
onstrated its usefulness, readers should also be mindful 
of some of MDS’s limitations compared to conventional 
neuropsychological tests. For example, conventional neu-
ropsychological testing usually evaluates both verbal and 
visual memory (e.g. using Craft Story 21 Delayed Recall 
and Benson Complex Figure Recall in this study); while 
MDS assess only verbal memory, which may reduce sen-
sitivity for detecting impairment in visual memory. As 
another example, unlike tests of executive function in 
conventional neuropsychological testing, MoCA–Execu-
tive includes a constellation of test items, some of which 
may not be specific to executive function and hence 
may affect MDS’s performance in identifying those with 
true impairment in executive function. Seventh, while 
the shorter version of MoCA–Memory still maintained 
excellent performance, readers should be mindful of 
the lack of cueing and recognition items in the shorter 
version (in contrast to the longer version), which may 
reduce its sensitivity for differentiating amnestic from 
non-amnestic (e.g., frontal/executive) memory profiles. 
Not uncommonly, impaired recall with intact recogni-
tion indicates a non-amnestic memory profile that is con-
sistent with problems in retrieval rather than storage of 
information; this pattern is often seen in subtypes of cog-
nitive impairment that affect executive function (e.g. vas-
cular, frontotemporal and Lewy Bodies subtypes) [1, 42].
Conclusions
This study developed a simple, Excel-based calcula-
tor to facilitate the conversion of MDS raw scores, 
approximating the age-, sex-, education-, and language-
adjusted Z-scores of conventional neuropsychological 
tests. The MDS Z-scores demonstrated excellent per-
formance in detecting impairment in the respective 
cognitive domains. They can potentially address two 
unmet needs in current clinical practices:
1)	 MDS provide a viable alternative when the conven-
tional neuropsychological testing is needed but can-
not be feasibly administered in clinical practice, 
such as in non-specialty clinics with large volume 
of patients at high-risk of cognitive impairment (e.g. 
primary-care, geriatric, and stroke-prevention clin-
ics), and, with further validation and calibration, 
plausibly also in resource-limited healthcare settings 
(e.g. in lower- and middle-income countries); and
2)	 While MDS may not fully substitute for conventional 
neuropsychological tests, they can complement 
neuropsychological testing as part of the systematic 
evaluation of cognitive impairment and help reserve 
neuropsychological tests for patients most likely to 
benefit from further evaluation.

Abstract: Background Test items in MoCA (Montreal Cognitive Assessment) can be used to generate 5 domain scores (i.e. Memory, Language, Attention, Executive and Visuospatial) which have been shown to approximate well-established neuropsychological tests. As neuropsychological tests are known to be affected by age, sex, education, and language of administration, this study derived a regression-based Z-score calculator for MoCA Domain Scores (MDS) that adjusts individual performance for these key confounders; with the intention of improving the clinical utility of MDS as a proxy for conventional neuropsychological tests. Methods Participants ≥ 50 years were recruited from Alzheimer’s Disease Centers across USA (n = 25,330), and com- pleted MoCA and conventional neuropsychological tests. A subset with normal cognition and global Clinical Demen- tia Rating of 0 (n = 11,371) was used to derive the Z-score calculator for MDS; while the full sample (n = 25,330) verified the performance of MDS Z-scores in detecting domain-specific impairments (as defined by conventional neuropsy- chological tests), using areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Results MDS varied significantly by age, sex, education, and language of administration even among participants with normal cognition. Based on age-, sex-, education-, and language-adjusted Z-scores, the respective AUCs were 91.2% for MoCA–Memory (95%CI 90.7–91.6), 83.6% for MoCA–Language (95%CI 83.0–84.3), 88.7% for MoCA–Atten- tion (95%CI 88.0–89.4), 85.5% for MoCA–Executive (95%CI 84.8–86.1), and 81.0% for MoCA–Visuospatial (95%CI 80.2–81.8). At the commonly-used cut-off of Z-scores ≤ -1.50, all the MDS had specificities of ≥ 80%. Conclusions MDS Z-scores can be easily computed using the newly-developed Excel-based calculator, and provide a viable alternative when conventional neuropsychological tests are needed but cannot be feasibly administered, such as in non-specialty clinics with large volume of patients at high-risk of cognitive impairment (e.g. primary-care, geriatric, and stroke-prevention clinics), and, with further validation and calibration, plausibly also in other resource- limited healthcare settings (e.g. in lower- and middle-income countries). They can complement neuropsychologi- cal tests as part of the systematic evaluation of cognitive impairment, and help reserve neuropsychological tests for patients most likely to benefit from further evaluation. *Correspondence: Tau Ming Liew liew.tau.ming@singhealth.com.sg; ephltm@nus.edu.sg Full list of author information is available at the end of the article Page 2 of 13 Liew ﻿Alzheimer’s Research & Therapy (2025) 17:167
